newsitem.title: FRANCE: France reluctantly backs Annan for top U.N. job.
newsitem.headline: France reluctantly backs Annan for top U.N. job.

text.p: France reluctantly backed Ghanaian Kofi Annan as new U.N. Secretary-General on Saturday after losing the latest battle in a war to keep up French influence in what it sees as a world dominated by Washington.

Angered by a U.S. veto of outgoing Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, Paris insisted a French speaker should get the job and had backed candidates from Francophone African countries before agreeing to English-speaking Annan.
By backing Annan, a U.N. career diplomat who speaks fluent French, Paris dropped threats of a tit-for-tat veto that would have further strained often fractious ties with Washington.
"Now that France has chosen Kofi Annan as its candidate, we will give him full and complete cooperation," Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said.

"It was normal for us to lend our support to candidates from (African) countries with links to France," before agreeing to Annan, he said. The 185-nation General Assembly will formally appoint Annan, who heads U.N. peacekeeping, on Tuesday.

Many foreign nations viewed Paris' insistence on a French speaker as quixotic, but it is symbolic of Paris' battle to maintain its clout against U.S. military and political might and the growing grip of the English language.

France works to block the flow of Hollywood movies and often coins French versions of Anglicisms. French, for centuries the language of diplomacy, is now the working language of the U.N. with English.
Losing out in Africa to Washington has an extra sting for Paris because it is a region where French political clout is strongest because of long colonial ties.

"France reacted very well. There has not been a single negative word from official French sources against me. I have no problem with France or French. I adore French culture," Annan said in remarks broadcast by France Info radio on Saturday.
Even Annan quipped about Paris' insistence on a Francophone.
In French marred for purists by the odd grammatical error, he said: "To be a true Francophone you have to speak English with a French accent. If I'm really pushed perhaps I can do it."

France, which often plays a role of gendarme in Africa, clashed with the United States over Zaire this year when it led an unsuccessful campaign to send a U.N. force to help Hutu refugees stranded by a Tutsi rebellion in eastern Zaire.

De Charette accused the world of being "spineless" in its reaction to the crisis, since defused by a homeward exodus of many refugees to Rwanda. Rwanda accused France of having a hidden agenda to bolster its interests in the region.
France is also at odds with Washington over a French call for a European to take over the southern command of NATO, traditionally held by a U.S. officer.

And in another spat over Africa, a French cabinet minister noted in October that U.S. President Bill Clinton had not visited Africa in four years and suggested that a trip by outgoing U.S. secretary of state Warren Christopher was a belated effort to show interest to help Clinton's re-election.
The left-leaning daily Liberation said that ditching Boutros-Ghali, a fluent French speaker who frequently visited Paris, and backing Annan "was not at all to France's taste."
It said France's insistence on a French speaker instead of Annan "hid the opposition to a candidate whose main fault was to have too clear backing from Washington and London."

"If one sticks to the official biographies, Kofi Annan was perhaps the worst choice," the conservative daily Le Figaro said. France's preferred candidates included Ivory Coast Foreign Minister Amara Essa.

But Le Figaro said it was "time to throw cold water on the Franco-U.S. fires" stoked this week by a row over whether de Charette walked out of a NATO function in Brussels to snub a farewell toast in honour of Christopher.
De Charette's office has said he did not know the tribute was due to take place but a U.S. official said he had been "extremely discourteous".
